Roles and responsibilities

Care and support workers

The responsibilities of care and support workers are to:

provide effective IPC practice in their day-to-day care

keep IPC skills and knowledge up to date

report any breaches in IPC precautions or measures, or any perceived risks that may lead to the spread of infection, to their registered manager (or nominated deputy) or office team leader

avoid providing care or having close contact with people accessing care and other staff if they feel unwell or have an infection that may pose a risk of spreading to others

ASC workers should always seek advice from their line manager and, where appropriate, medical advice before returning to or continuing with duties

Registered managers, office team leaders and supervisors

The responsibilities of ASC setting managers and supervisors are to:

ensure all staff deliver effective IPC practice in their day-to-day care delivery, protecting themselves and reducing the risk of infection to people, colleagues, and others they come into contact with

ensure Health and Social Care Act 2008 is followed

ensure all staff have completed IPC training and that the training is kept up to date

ensure sufficient support and resources are available for staff to implement, monitor and take corrective action in line with this guidance

ensure risk assessments are carried out on any staff who may be at high risk of complications from infection (for example, pregnant staff)

support and encourage staff to have recommended health checks and immunisations, documenting any risks and adjusting duties as needed

conduct regular IPC audits of infection prevention practices to provide assurance of compliance with this guidance

assess risks and coordinate contact with General Practitioner (GP), UKHSA local HPT, or IPC services as required

Useful tools for ASC managers and supervisors include:

CQC Adult social care inspection information gathering tool: on infection prevention and control

HSE resource on how to identify hazards and assess risks at work

Scottish national monitoring framework to support safe and clean care audit programmes: An organisational approach to prevention of infection auditing

NHS Integrated Care Boards (ICBs) and public health teams supporting ASC

ICBs hold overall responsibility for infection prevention across health and social care in their local area (as per Health and Social Care Act 2008: code of practice on the prevention and control of infections). Their legal responsibilities are to:

commission services for ‘prevention of illness’ and ‘care of persons suffering from illness’ (noting that the ICB remit is much broader than IPC)

ensure providers comply with statutory infection control law, including the Health and Social Care Act 2008 Code of Practice

hold system‑wide accountability for quality performance (effectiveness, safety, experience) across the integrated care systems (ICS)

Healthcare services supporting the ASC sector

Healthcare services play an important role in supporting the ASC sector by working collaboratively with care providers to ensure safe, coordinated and person-centred care. This includes timely access to clinical assessment, treatment and specialist support, including end of life, effective hospital discharge and prevention of avoidable admissions. Clear communication and information sharing between health and ASC services is essential to ensure continuity of care and improve outcomes for people who access care and support.

Community IPC teams

Community IPC teams are specialist teams that provide expert advice and support on preventing and managing infections in ASC settings. They may be employed or commissioned by the NHS or local authorities.

The responsibilities of community IPC Teams where commissioned are to:

provide hands-on IPC expertise and support for front-line ASC providers to help them implement best IPC practice

provide direct support to ASC settings for outbreaks and/or infection incidents

communicate with UKHSA HPTs where necessary

UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA)

The responsibilities of UKHSA at a national level are to:

prevent and reduce the harm caused by infectious diseases

provide leadership and clear IPC guidance that helps keep people safe, well and supported

monitor infection and outbreak data to track the spread of disease

UKHSA Health Protection Teams (HPTs) (regional level)

UKHSA HPTs provide specialist public health advice and operational support to NHS, local authorities and other agencies.

UKHSA HPTs lead the UKHSA response to local outbreaks and incidents at a regional level and may provide advice and support for single cases of notifiable diseases. They track infections, learn how they spread, and give clear, practical advice to help stop people getting ill.

The extent of UKSHA HPT involvement in outbreak and incident management may vary slightly between HPT regions depending on local public health infrastructure, local risk profiles, ASC system capacity, and regional operational arrangements.

UKHSA HPTs do not have a performance management or assurance role within the regional or local health system. Their role is advisory and supportive, working in partnership with ASC providers to help manage public health risks effectively and in line with national guidance.

Local authority

Local authorities have a legal duty to protect and improve the health of people in their area. They help prevent and manage infections by working with local partners and supporting IPC.

They are responsible for coordinating local outbreak responses, ensuring the provision of environmental health services, and maintaining emergency preparedness through local resilience forums.

The term ‘care and support workers’ is also used throughout to refer to all ASC workers/staff.

Safeguarding statement

In keeping with the Mental Capacity Act 2005, care and support workers must presume capacity unless assessed otherwise, provide tailored support to enable understanding, and document any capacity assessments clearly. Where a person lacks capacity, decisions or protective measures must be made in their best interests and be proportionate, necessary, and least restrictive, with involvement from relevant professionals and those close to the person wherever appropriate.

Always ensure any information sharing about a person who is infectious is done in a compassionate and proportionate way.
